title: How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?
shortTitle: How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?

s1_definition.profdef: A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a `.log` file holding a contiguous range of records by offset, accompanied by an offset index `.index` file that maps offsets to byte positions in the log, and a time index `.timeindex` file that maps timestamps to offsets. Only the newest segment, the active segment, is written to; older segments are closed and immutable. Retention and compaction operate at the granularity of these closed segments: time or size retention deletes whole aged segments, and compaction rewrites closed segments to keep only the latest record per key, while the active segment is left untouched.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a partition's transaction history in a filing cabinet, where each drawer is a segment holding a block of consecutive entries. Each drawer has a small index card on the front that says "entry number so-and-so starts at this spot in the drawer," so a clerk can jump straight to an entry instead of reading the whole drawer; that is the offset index. There is also a second card mapping dates to entry numbers; that is the time index. Clerks only ever add new entries to the front drawer that is currently open; the older drawers are sealed and never changed. When it is time to clean up, the bank either throws out whole sealed drawers that are too old, which is retention, or rewrites sealed drawers to keep only the latest entry for each account, which is compaction, and in both cases they never touch the open front drawer.
s1_definition.oneliner: A partition is a directory of immutable closed segments plus one active segment, each segment paired with an offset index and a time index, and retention deletes whole aged segments while compaction rewrites closed segments to the latest-per-key, never touching the active segment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a `.log` file holding a contiguous range of records by offset, accompanied by an offset index `.index` file that maps offsets to byte positions in the log, and a time index `.timeindex` file that maps timestamps to offsets. Only the newest segment, the active segment, is written to; older segments are closed and immutable. Retention and compaction operate at the granularity of these closed segments: time or size retention deletes whole aged segments, and compaction rewrites closed segments to keep only the latest record per key, while the active segment is left untouched.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a partition's transaction history in a filing cabinet, where each drawer is a segment holding a block of consecutive entries. Each drawer has a small index card on the front that says "entry number so-and-so starts at this spot in the drawer," so a clerk can jump straight to an entry instead of reading the whole drawer; that is the offset index. There is also a second card mapping dates to entry numbers; that is the time index. Clerks only ever add new entries to the front drawer that is currently open; the older drawers are sealed and never changed. When it is time to clean up, the bank either throws out whole sealed drawers that are too old, which is retention, or rewrites sealed drawers to keep only the latest entry for each account, which is compaction, and in both cases they never touch the open front drawer.

**One line to remember:** A partition is a directory of immutable closed segments plus one active segment, each segment paired with an offset index and a time index, and retention deletes whole aged segments while compaction rewrites closed segments to the latest-per-key, never touching the active segment.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the on-disk layout. For a topic partition, Kafka creates a directory named like `topicname-0` for partition zero. Inside it are groups of three files per segment, named by the base offset of the segment, for example `00000000000000000000.log`, `00000000000000000000.index`, and `00000000000000000000.timeindex`. The `.log` file is the actual record data, a sequence of record batches appended in offset order. The `.index` file is the offset index, and the `.timeindex` file is the time index. A partition therefore looks like a series of these triples, one per segment, with the highest-base-offset segment being the active one.

The offset index exists to make reads fast. The `.log` file can be a gigabyte, so to find the record at a given offset without scanning, Kafka keeps the offset index, which is a sparse map from a logical offset to the physical byte position in the `.log` file where that offset's batch begins. It is sparse, meaning it does not have an entry for every record but one roughly every few kilobytes, controlled by `index.interval.bytes`, so to read offset N, Kafka binary-searches the index for the nearest indexed offset at or below N, seeks to that byte position in the log, and scans forward a short distance to N. This makes a lookup cheap while keeping the index small. The time index similarly maps timestamps to offsets so that operations like "seek to the first message after this time" and time-based retention can work efficiently.

Now segment rolling. The active segment keeps growing as producers append. Kafka closes it and starts a new active segment when the active segment reaches `segment.bytes` in size or `segment.ms` in age, whichever comes first. When a segment is closed, it becomes immutable; nothing is ever appended to or modified in a closed segment. This immutability is what makes retention and compaction safe and simple, because they only ever operate on segments that will not change under them, and it is why the active segment is always excluded from cleanup.

Retention interacts with segments by deleting whole segments. With `cleanup.policy=delete`, Kafka checks closed segments against the retention policy: a segment is eligible for deletion when all its records are older than `retention.ms`, judged by the segment's largest timestamp, or when the partition's total size exceeds `retention.bytes` and the oldest segments must go to fit. Crucially, retention never deletes individual records; it deletes entire segment files, so retention granularity is the segment. This is why segment size matters for retention precision: smaller segments let retention trim data closer to the exact cutoff, while a large segment cannot be deleted until its very last record ages out.

Compaction interacts with segments by rewriting them. With `cleanup.policy=compact`, the log cleaner scans the closed segments, builds a map of the latest offset per key, and rewrites the closed segments into new, smaller segments that keep only the most recent record for each key, plus tombstones within their retention window. It processes the dirty portion of the log, the closed segments that have accumulated enough stale updates per the `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio`, and it never touches the active segment. Compaction preserves offsets, meaning the surviving records keep their original offsets even though intermediate offsets are now gone, so the log can have gaps in offset numbering after compaction, which consumers handle transparently. A topic can also be `compact,delete`, in which case both apply: the cleaner compacts closed segments and retention still deletes whole segments that age out.

Putting the interaction together: both retention and compaction are segment-oriented background operations that only touch closed, immutable segments and always skip the active segment. Retention is coarse, operating by deleting whole segments based on age or size. Compaction is finer within a key but still works segment by segment, rewriting closed segments to the latest value per key. The offset and time indexes are maintained alongside, rebuilt for the rewritten segments after compaction and deleted along with their segment on retention.

Senior-level nuances. Segment size is a central tuning knob with competing effects: smaller segments give finer retention and let compaction and cleanup run in smaller, smoother bursts, but they add file-handle and index overhead and more frequent rolling, while larger segments are more efficient for steady-state append and read but make retention coarser and cleanup burstier. The active segment is never eligible for retention or compaction, so a very low-traffic partition whose active segment rarely rolls can retain data far longer than `retention.ms` suggests, until `segment.ms` forces a roll. After a broker restart Kafka may rebuild or sanity-check indexes from the log, which is why index files are treated as reconstructable rather than authoritative. And compaction's offset-preserving rewrite is why you can rely on a specific key's latest value always being present while older offsets for that key simply vanish.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India stores two kinds of streams: the `account.ledger` topic for an append-only transaction history under delete retention, and the `account.state` topic for the latest balance per account under compaction. Rajesh is SAV2001 and Priya is CUR3001. The team needed to understand exactly how segments, indexes, retention, and compaction behave to tune disk usage and reason about what data survives.

Problem 1 — the ops team saw multiple `.log`, `.index`, and `.timeindex` files per partition and did not understand the layout or why some old data was deleted in chunks rather than record by record. This is the segment-and-index layout plus the fact that retention deletes whole segments.

Problem 2 — on the compacted `account.state` topic they noticed offset gaps and wanted to confirm that the latest balance per account was always retained. This is compaction rewriting closed segments to the latest-per-key while preserving and skipping offsets.

Our runnable demo models a `Partition` made of `Segment` objects each with a log, an offset index, and a time index, an active segment that cannot be cleaned, a `RetentionPolicy` that deletes aged segments, and a `Compactor` that rewrites closed segments to latest-per-key. It shows an offset-index lookup, a retention pass, and a compaction pass with resulting offset gaps. The classes are `SegmentStorageDemo`, `LogRecord`, `OffsetIndex`, `Segment`, `Partition`, `RetentionPolicy`, and `Compactor`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an `account.ledger` partition with two closed segments and one active segment, and an `account.state` compacted partition.

Step 1: On disk the ledger partition is a directory containing, for each segment, a `.log` file of records, a `.index` offset-index file, and a `.timeindex` time-index file, named by the segment's base offset. The highest-base-offset segment is the active one that producers are still appending to; the others are closed and immutable.

Step 2: To read offset four, Kafka finds the segment whose offset range contains four, binary-searches that segment's sparse offset index for the nearest indexed offset at or below four, seeks to that byte position in the `.log`, and scans forward a short distance to offset four. The sparse index keeps lookups cheap without storing an entry per record.

Step 3: A retention pass runs with a cutoff. Each closed segment is checked by its largest timestamp, and any segment whose records are all older than the cutoff is deleted as a whole file, along with its index and time index. Retention never removes individual records; its granularity is the whole segment, and the active segment is never eligible.

Step 4: On the compacted `account.state` partition, the compactor scans the closed segments, builds the latest record per key, and rewrites the closed segments to keep only those latest records. SAV2001 had three versions across offsets zero, two, and three; only offset three survives, so offsets zero and two disappear and the log now has gaps in offset numbering, which is normal because compaction preserves the surviving records' original offsets.

Step 5: Throughout, the active segment is left untouched by both retention and compaction, which is why both operations are safe and simple, and it also means a low-traffic partition can keep data longer than its retention time suggests until the active segment finally rolls. The combination gives the ledger a bounded, segment-granular history and the state topic a guaranteed latest-value-per-key store.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Partition directory: account.ledger-0/
    │
    ├─ 00000000000000000000.log  (+ .index + .timeindex)  [closed, immutable]
    ├─ 00000000000000000003.log  (+ .index + .timeindex)  [closed, immutable]
    └─ 00000000000000000005.log  (+ .index + .timeindex)  [ACTIVE — appends go here]

  READ offset 4:
    find segment [base 3] -> offset index floor(4)=3 -> seek byte pos -> scan fwd -> record 4

  RETENTION (cleanup.policy=delete):
    closed segment maxTs <= cutoff ? delete WHOLE .log/.index/.timeindex  (active skipped)

  COMPACTION (cleanup.policy=compact):
    scan CLOSED segments -> latest record per key -> rewrite closed segments
    surviving offsets preserved -> offset GAPS appear (active skipped)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a dot-log file holding a contiguous range of records in offset order, and it is paired with a dot-index offset index and a dot-timeindex time index, all named by the segment's base offset. Only the newest segment, the active segment, is written to; all older segments are closed and immutable. That immutability is the foundation that makes everything else safe.

The offset index exists so reads are fast without scanning gigabyte files. It is a sparse map from logical offset to the physical byte position in the log, with one entry roughly every few kilobytes controlled by the index interval, so to read a given offset Kafka binary-searches the index for the nearest indexed offset at or below it, seeks to that byte position, and scans forward a short way. The time index does the same for timestamps, which is what powers time-based seeks and time retention. Kafka rolls the active segment into a closed one when it hits the configured segment size or segment age, and from that moment the segment never changes.

Retention and compaction both operate at segment granularity on closed segments and always skip the active segment. Delete retention deletes whole segments: a closed segment is removed when all its records are older than the retention time, judged by its largest timestamp, or when the partition exceeds its size limit and the oldest segments must go. It never deletes individual records, which is why retention is coarse and why segment size controls how precisely you can trim data. Compaction instead rewrites closed segments: the log cleaner builds the latest record per key across the dirty closed segments and rewrites them to keep only those latest records plus tombstones within their window, preserving the surviving records' original offsets, so after compaction the log legitimately has gaps in offset numbering. A topic can be both compact and delete, in which case the cleaner compacts closed segments and retention still deletes whole aged ones.

On the National Bank of India systems this maps cleanly: the append-only ledger topic uses delete retention so old history is trimmed by dropping whole aged segments, and the account-state topic uses compaction so the latest balance per account is always retained while older versions vanish, which is exactly the offset-gap behavior we saw and confirmed was correct. The nuances I always mention are that segment size is a trade-off, since smaller segments give finer retention and smoother cleanup bursts but more file and index overhead, while larger segments are more efficient but coarser; that the active segment is never cleaned, so a low-traffic partition can hold data longer than its retention time until the segment finally rolls; and that index files are treated as reconstructable from the log, which is why a broker can rebuild them on restart. The one-line principle is that a partition is a sequence of immutable segments plus one active segment, each with a sparse offset and time index, and all cleanup is segment-oriented, which is what makes Kafka's storage both fast to read and simple to clean.
